name: Biafada
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 4 other works read were silent
catalog_citation: Wilson, W. A. A. 1993. An outline description of Biafada. Journal of West African Languages 23(2): 59-90.
catalog_locator: sec. 1.3 'Tone and stress', p. 63 (PDF page 5 of 32; scanned; page re-rendered at 130 dpi by the third reader, quote checked against the image)
catalog_quote: 1.3 TONE AND STRESS There clearly are both a tone system and a dynamic stress accent, but research time did not permit this to be explored. Neither tone nor stress seem to carry a very great information load, since minimal pairs distinguished by one or the other are very few, and the commonest ones were well known and joked about. An initial high tone followed by a low tone sounds stressed, including when it is on a noun class prefix, as in bú-lənnä ‘snake’. Errors in tone or stress impede comprehension rather than conveying wrong or zero meaning, and my errors of stress were firmly corrected when reading back transcribed examples.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (32 pp, image-only scan, the PDF's metadata gives the title JWAL-23-2-Wilson.tif) and rendered PDF page 5 (printed p. 63) and page 1 (p. 59) to PNG. Page 63 carries the heading '1.3 TONE AND STRESS' followed by exactly the two paragraphs quoted in the report, word for word, including 'bú-lənnä ‘snake’' (the scanned file lines 258-269 has 'bi-lanna'; the reader's correction from the page image is right). The reader's reading is sound: the source asserts both a tone system and a dynamic stress accent, says explicitly that they were not explored, and gives no placement rule; the only observation is that an initial H-L contour is perceived as stress, even on a class prefix. new_statements.rule_in_words: The source asserts that Biafada has both lexical tone and a dynamic stress accent but gives no placement rule: stress was not studied. The one observation is that a word-initial high tone followed by a low tone is perceived as stress, even when the initial syllable is a noun-class prefix (bú-lənnä 'snake'), i.e. perceived stress tracks an initial H-L tonal contour rather than a fixed syllable. Minimal pairs for tone or stress are said to be very few.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author explicitly says the tone/stress system was not explored. Elsewhere (p. 69) a tonal difference (high tone on the first syllable) is noted between the 2sg subject suffix -ra and the invariable marker -re.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated nouns and verb forms elicited from one consultant, Sambu Chambu, at Empada, 1992); no phrase-level or citation-form discussion. Verified against the page image; scanned of the example corrected to bú-lənnä.
new_statements.identity_note: Wilson 1993 describes the Biafada (self-name Ganjoola) of Empada, southern Guinea-Bissau, from one consultant (1992 fieldwork plus 1959 wordlists); no dialect is named. Lopes 2023 names four dialects (binala, bubwas, cacandé, buwol). Glottolog biaf1240 has no dialect subdivisions, so the statement maps to the language-level code.
